title: FlowNIB: An Information Bottleneck Analysis of Bidirectional vs. Unidirectional Language Models
claim: Layerwise training trajectories in the information plane reveal how representations compress and retain task information, differing across architectures.
layout: 2 side-by-side plot panels, epoch colorbars, green optimal-coordinate line overlaid on layer curves
description: Two side-by-side information-plane plots. The left panel is DeBERTaV3-Base and the right is MobileLLM-350M, both on MRPC. The x-axis is I(X;Z) and the y-axis is I(Z;Y). Each panel shows a stack of smooth curves, one per layer, shifted horizontally by a small constant offset so they separate. The curves are colored by training epoch on a yellow-to-purple gradient (0 to 2000), with a colorbar at the right of each panel. Early epochs (yellow) sit low, and later epochs (purple) climb higher on I(Z;Y). A thick green line with dark-green circular markers connects the optimal information coordinate across layers. It rises smoothly in the left panel. In the right panel it is jagged and noisy. The eye goes first to the bold green line over the colorful fan of curves.
caption: Information-plane trajectories under FlowNIB training for (left) DeBERTaV3-Base and (right) MobileLLM-350M on MRPC. Each curve shows mutual information I(Z; Y ) versus I(X; Z) over training epochs, colored by epoch progression. A constant offset of +0.05 is added to I(X; Z) for each successive layer to visually separate the layerwise trajectories. The green line represents the Optimal Information Coordinate (OIC) across layers.
abstract: Bidirectional language models have better context understanding and perform better than unidirectional models on natural language understanding tasks, yet the theoretical reasons behind this advantage remain unclear. In this work, we investigate this disparity through the lens of the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle, which formalizes a trade-off between compressing input information and preserving task-relevant content. We propose FlowNIB, a dynamic and scalable method for estimating mutual information during training that addresses key limitations of classical IB approaches, including computational intractability and fixed trade-off schedules. Theoretically, we show that bidirectional models retain more mutual information and exhibit higher effective dimensionality than unidirectional models. To support this, we present a generalized framework for measuring representational complexity and prove that bidirectional representations are strictly more informative under mild conditions. We further validate our findings through extensive experiments across multiple models and tasks using FlowNIB, revealing how information is encoded and compressed throughout training. Together, our work provides a principled explanation for the effectiveness of bidirectional architectures and introduces a practical tool for analyzing information flow in deep language models.
